Utility is not identical to the cash payout
Rejecting money to punish unfairness violates the cash-maximizing model if money is the only valued outcome. If fairness, reciprocity or expressive conduct enters utility, the act need not violate expected-utility theory. The essay partially acknowledges this; its moral criticism must therefore defend the values or consequences, not borrow a theorem’s authority.

High stakes change the picture, but do not erase all rejection
Cameron did report a participant rejecting an offer worth about a month’s expenditure. The study also found greater willingness to accept a given percentage at higher stakes. The anecdote is real; using it without that comparative result conceals how price-sensitive the behavior was. Fairness motives and monetary stakes both matter.
Cameron (1999)

The ancestral group-size story explains too much too easily
A fixed small-band picture does not establish why a modern person resists joining a large organization. Hill and colleagues describe mobile, interconnected residence patterns across contemporary foraging societies; these are indirect evidence, not a census of ancestors. The specific psychological adaptation claimed here remains unmeasured.
Hill et al. (2011)

Positive benefit is not enough when better options exist
The author acknowledges opportunity cost and then discounts its practical relevance. A project can offer positive value while being a poor use of limited attention or funds. That is especially important in a book that elsewhere urges rigorous comparison among charities: the standard should not weaken when the reader is asked to join the author’s kind of organization.
